title: My Lazy Sourdough Method (No Stretch and Folds)
creator: Nadia Okafor
description:
The sourdough I actually make on weeknights. No stretch and folds, no stress.

Recipe:
500g bread flour
375g water
100g active starter
10g salt

Mix, rest, salt, bulk 5-6 hours, shape, fridge overnight, bake at 250C covered 20 min, uncovered 20 min.

Instagram: @nadiabakes

sentences.t: Hi friends, welcome back to the kitchen.
Today I'm showing you the sourdough I actually make on a Tuesday night when I have zero energy.
No stretch and folds, no alarms every thirty minutes, no drama.
Just a really good loaf with about ten minutes of actual hands on time.
So, starter first.
This is Gerald, he's four years old, and he lives in my fridge.
I fed him last night before bed, and you can see he's nice and bubbly and he's doubled.
If you drop a little spoonful in water and it floats, you're good to go.
Look at that, floating, beautiful, good job Gerald.
Into the big bowl goes five hundred grams of bread flour and three hundred seventy five grams of water.
I'm just squishing it together with my hand until there's no dry flour left.
It's going to look shaggy and ugly and that is exactly right.
Now I add the starter, a hundred grams, and squish again.
Then a cover, and we leave it alone for half an hour.
After the rest, the salt goes in, ten grams, with just a splash of water to help it dissolve.
And this is where the lazy part comes in.
Instead of stretch and folds, I do one really good knead right in the bowl for about two minutes, and then I don't touch it again.
The long, slow bulk does the work for you, the gluten builds up on its own while you go live your life.
So now we wait five to six hours, depending on how warm your kitchen is.

I tip it out onto a barely floured counter.
Pre shape into a loose round, and leave it for twenty minutes.
Then the final shape, I fold the sides in, roll it up toward me, and drag it to build some tension on the top.
Into a towel lined bowl that I've dusted with rice flour, seam side up.
Rice flour is the secret, by the way, it doesn't stick like regular flour does.
Then it goes in the fridge overnight, covered with a shower cap, which is the best kitchen tool I own.

The oven is at two fifty Celsius with the Dutch oven inside, and it's been heating for forty five minutes.
I flip the dough straight from the fridge onto parchment, and score it with one long, confident slash.
Okay, maybe medium confident.
Lid on, twenty minutes.
Lid off, another twenty, until it's deep, deep brown.
People pull their bread out way too pale, so trust me, darker is better.
And here she is.
Listen to that crackling, that's the crust cooling down.
You have to wait at least an hour before cutting, I know, I know.

Look at that crumb, nice and open, a little shiny, not gummy at all.
Ten minutes of work, and that's the loaf.
If you try this, tag me, I want to see your Geralds.
See you next week, friends.
